query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of high‐melting-point dopants (specifically yttrium and hafnium) to the uniform, fine‐lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy will jointly improve its mechanical properties (strength, ductility, and creep resistance) and its resistance to high‐temperature corrosion through dopant-induced segregation that fosters the formation of protective oxide scales and microstructural stabilization via sluggish diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy in a uniform, fine lamellar state with strength and plasticity below industrial application requirements.
generation.intervention: Introduce low-level Y and Hf dopants in controlled amounts into the alloy via controlled alloying (or alternatively via a co-doped surface modification process such as laser cladding) to modify the chemistry at phase boundaries and in the matrix.
generation.conditions: Performance is evaluated under cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations (from ambient to very high temperatures), long-term mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and exposure to corrosive environments such as chloride-containing solutions and molten salt conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The Y and Hf atoms are expected to segregate at phase boundaries and in grain interiors, promoting the formation of more stable, adherent oxide layers and inhibiting grain growth, which refines the microstructure and strengthens semi-coherent interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The dopants modify the local chemistry to stabilize the lamellar structure during thermal cycling and reduce diffusion-mediated coarsening, leveraging the sluggish diffusion characteristic of high-entropy alloys; they also aid in the formation of protective oxide scales that are resistant to spallation during high-temperature corrosion, while a refined microstructure and robust phase boundaries enhance dislocation storage and back-stress strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped, as-cast alloy, the Y+Hf-modified alloy will exhibit higher yield and ultimate strengths, improved plasticity (ductility), reduced room-temperature creep rate, and enhanced resistance to high-temperature corrosion and oxide scale spallation.
generation.baseline: The original, uniform fine-lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without any Y/Hf doping.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be effective for fasteners operating under temperature cycles from room temperature up to ~900°C and under corrosive conditions typical of chloride-containing solutions or molten salts. Mechanical tests should mimic long-term loading and creep conditions relevant to industrial fastener applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise dopant concentrations for optimal performance and the quantitative performance improvements remain to be determined. Additionally, interactions between enhanced corrosion resistance and ductility need careful evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of alloy samples using identical thermo-mechanical processing: one set of the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set doped with the designated amounts of Y and Hf. Subject both sets to accelerated aging cycles with thermal fluctuations (room temperature to ~900°C), long-term static and cyclic mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep tests), and high-temperature corrosion tests in aggressive media (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid and molten salt environments).
measurements: Tensile and compressive strength and ductility (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Room-temperature creep rates under fixed loads
Hot corrosion performance (oxide scale adherence, spallation area, mass loss/weight gain)
Microstructural analyses (grain size, phase stability, and dopant segregation via SEM/TEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped samples do not display statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (enhanced strength and ductility, reduced creep rate) and corrosion resistance relative to the undoped baseline under the defined operating conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. Due to their unique solid solution structures, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) typically exhibit various excellent properties, such as high strength/hardness [,,,], high wear resistance [], outstanding temperature strength [], strong structural stability [], good corrosion resistance [,], and oxidation resistance [] Generally speaking, HEAs can be divided into face-centered cubic (FCC) HEAs, body-centered cubic (BCC) HEAs, FCC + BCC two-phase HEAs, etc., from the perspective of phase structure. The high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a single FCC structure has high ductility but low hardness. For example, the CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a room temperature fracture elongation of 52%, but a tensile strength of only 563 MPa [], and the Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy has a tensile ductility of 58%, but a yield strength of only 240 MPa []. Although HEA with a single BCC structure has high strength and hardness, it also has low ductility. Therefore, an important challenge in the engineering application of high-entropy alloys is how to obtain high strength and high ductility at the same time.
